reasons: The lake identity record gives case_name Carpenter v. United States, court U.S. Supreme Court, date_decided 2018-06-22, and year 2018.
The lake citations record official citation 585 U.S. 296, parallel citations 138 S. Ct. 2206 and 201 L. Ed. 2d 507, and vendor neutral citation 2018 U.S. LEXIS 3844.

defect.locator_note: The opinion supports the CSLI dividing-line role; the disclosed files do not supply evidence for the internal A6 designation.
defect.problem: The legal role as a key CSLI/third-party-doctrine dividing-line case is supported, but the parenthetical sublocator 'A6' is not verifiable from the disclosed authority record, opinion text, inventory, or content page body.
defect.proposed_fix: Use 'Key — CSLI dividing line (co-home)' unless a disclosed home-page taxonomy verifies the A6 locator.

reasons: The opinion states that the third-party doctrine applies to telephone numbers and bank records but that CSLI is a 'qualitatively different category of cell-site records.'
The Court says, 'We decline to extend Smith and Miller to cover these novel circumstances,' which supports the case's key role on Third-Party Doctrine & CSLI.
residual_risks: A separate home-page or taxonomy file would be needed to verify 'A6' as an internal locator.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Remove '(A6)' from this role unless the corpus discloses the home-section taxonomy.

defect.evidence_quote: Nor do we address other business records that might incidentally reveal location information.
defect.problem: The core holding is supported, but the phrasing 'narrows the third-party doctrine for digital-age data' is broader than the opinion's narrow CSLI/location-data holding, and the quoted phrase 'the whole of [one's] physical movements' is not character-faithful to the opinion's wording.
defect.proposed_fix: Revise to: 'Acquiring at least seven days of historical CSLI is a Fourth Amendment search; an individual has a legitimate expectation of privacy in the record of his physical movements as captured through CSLI; Carpenter declines to extend Smith and Miller to digital-age location data/CSLI.'

reasons: The opinion directly supports the search holding: 'The location information obtained from Carpenter’s wireless carriers was the product of a search.'
The opinion supports a narrower third-party rule: 'We therefore decline to extend Smith and Miller to the collection of CSLI.'
The exact opinion wording is 'the whole of their physical movements' and later 'the whole of his physical movements,' not 'the whole of [one's] physical movements.'
residual_risks: The page's separate Rule quote and pin-op11 are not separate inventory rows here, though the lake pinpoint is marked quote_fidelity=mismatch.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Replace 'digital-age data' with 'digital-age location data' or 'CSLI' and use an exact quotation or paraphrase rather than the bracketed '[one's]' quote.

reasons: The opinion frames the case through Katz reasonable-expectation doctrine and states that 'official intrusion into that private sphere generally qualifies as a search.'

The Court holds that an individual maintains a legitimate expectation of privacy in the record of physical movements captured through CSLI, supporting a key refinement role under Reasonable Expectation of Privacy.
Lens A does not audit treatment/currency, but the authority-weight label is supported by the lake identity fields: court U.S. Supreme Court, court_level scotus.
A Supreme Court authority-weight label of Binding — SCOTUS matches the disclosed identity record.
residual_risks: Substantive treatment/currency review is reserved to Lens B.

reasons: Lens A does not raise treatment findings; the payload matches the disclosed lake treatment fields: field_i_validity good_law, as_of_content 2018-06-22, as_of_treatment 2026-06-30, composite_basis migration-seed, and varies_by_point false.
The scope note's legal description is also supportable from the opinion's CSLI-specific narrowing of Smith and Miller.
residual_risks: Substantive treatment/currency review is reserved to Lens B.
